sections.title: Chapter 1
sections.subtitle: Prologue: The Desire for Mystical Peace and the Vision of the Seraph on Mount La Verna

content.text: 1. In the beginning I call upon the First Beginning, from Whom all illumination descends as from the Father of lights, from Whom are all the best gifts and all the perfect gifts, the Eternal Father through His Son our Lord Jesus Christ, that by the intercession of the most Holy Virgin Mary, Mother of the same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Blessed Francis, our father and leader, He may enlighten the eyes of our mind to guide our feet into the way of that peace which surpasses all understanding: that peace which our Lord Jesus Christ announced and gave to His disciples, which also our father Francis proclaimed in all his preachings, always announcing peace in every salutation, wishing peace to men and women, to the little and to the great.

2. Moved by the example of our most blessed father Francis, I sought after this peace with an ardent longing—I a sinner who, though in all things unworthy, have succeeded after his death as the seventh Minister General of the Friars. And so it happened that thirty-three years after the passing of the Blessed Father, about the time of his feast, by divine impulse I withdrew to Mount La Verna as to a quiet place, desiring to seek peace of soul. While I was meditating there upon the various ascents of the soul to God, among other things there occurred to me that miracle which in that very place happened to Blessed Francis himself: the vision of the six-winged Seraph in the likeness of the Crucified. Meditating upon this, I saw at once that this vision represented not only the contemplation of the Patriarch himself in ecstasy, but also the road by which that contemplation is attained.

3. For by those six wings are rightly understood the six stages of illumination by which the soul, as if by certain steps or journeys, is disposed to pass over into peace through the ecstatic transports of Christian wisdom. Now the road is only through the most ardent love of the Crucified, which so transformed Paul into Christ when he was caught up to the third heaven that he could say: "With Christ I am nailed to the cross; but I live, yet now not I, but Christ liveth in me." This same love so absorbed the mind of Francis that his spirit shone forth through his flesh when for two years before his death he bore the most holy stigmata of the Passion in his body. The six wings of the Seraph, therefore, symbolize the six levels of illumination that begin with creatures and lead us even into God, into Whom no one rightly enters except through the Crucified.

4. For he who does not enter by the door, but climbeth up another way, the same is a thief and a robber. But if anyone enter in by this door, he shall go in and go out, and shall find pastures. Therefore Saint John says in the Apocalypse: "Blessed are they that wash their robes in the blood of the Lamb, that they may have the right to the tree of life, and may enter in by the gates into the city." It is as if he said that into the heavenly Jerusalem no one can enter by contemplation unless he enters through the Blood of the Lamb as through a gate. For no one is in any way disposed for divine contemplation that leads to spiritual ecstasy unless, like Daniel, he is a man of desires. But desires are kindled in us in two ways: namely, by the cry of prayer that makes us roar from the grief of our heart, and by the radiance of contemplation whereby the mind turns itself most directly and intensely toward the rays of divine light.

5. Wherefore, to the cry of prayer through Christ crucified, in Whose blood we are cleansed from the filth of our sins, I first of all invite the reader, lest perchance he should believe that it suffices to have reading without unction, speculation without devotion, investigation without admiration, circumspection without exultation, industry without piety, knowledge without charity, intelligence without humility, study without divine grace, or the mirror without divinely inspired wisdom. To those, therefore, who are already predisposed by divine grace, to the humble and the pious, to those who sorrow for their sins and are devout, to those who are anointed with the oil of gladness, to the lovers of divine wisdom and those inflamed with desire for it, to those who wish to give themselves to praising, admiring, and tasting God, I propose the following considerations, reminding them that the mirror presented from without profits little unless the mirror of our mind be cleansed and polished. Exercise yourself, therefore, man of God, before you lift up your eyes to the rays of Wisdom reflecting in these mirrors, lest by chance you fall into a deeper pit of darkness through beholding them with an unpurified eye.

sections.title: Chapter 2
sections.subtitle: Chapter I: On the Stages of the Ascent to God and on His Contemplation through His Vestiges in the Universe

content.text: 1. Blessed is the man whose help is from Thee; in his heart he hath disposed to ascend by steps, in the vale of tears, in the place which he hath set. Since happiness is nothing else than the enjoyment of the Supreme Good, and the Supreme Good is above us, no one can be made happy unless he rise above himself, not by an ascent of the body, but of the heart. Yet we cannot be raised above ourselves unless a higher power elevate us. No matter how much our interior steps are disposed, nothing is accomplished unless divine aid accompanies us. But divine aid accompanies those who seek it from their heart with humility and devotion; and this is to sigh for it in this vale of tears, which is done through fervent prayer. Prayer, therefore, is the mother and origin of the upward ascent in God.

2. Since, then, prayer is the mother and beginning of ascent, Dionysius in his Mystical Theology, wishing to instruct us in mystical transports, puts prayer first. Let us therefore pray to the Lord our God: "Lead me, O Lord, in Thy way, and I will walk in Thy truth; let my heart rejoice that it may fear Thy name." In praying this prayer, we are enlightened to know the steps of the divine ascent. For since, according to our present condition, the universe of things is a ladder by which we may ascend into God, and since among created things some are vestiges, some images, some corporeal, some spiritual, some temporal, some everlasting, and consequently some outside us, some within us, and some above us; in order that we may arrive at the contemplation of the First Beginning, Who is purely spiritual, eternal, and above us, we must pass through the vestiges, which are corporeal, temporal, and outside us, and this is to be led in the way of God.

3. We must also enter into our mind, which is the image of God, everlasting, spiritual, and within us; and this is to walk in the truth of God. We must finally pass beyond to that which is eternal, purely spiritual, and above us, looking to the First Principle; and this is to rejoice in the knowledge of God and in the reverence of His majesty. This is the three-day journey in the wilderness; this is the threefold illumination of a single day: the first is like evening, the second like morning, the third like midday. This corresponds to the threefold existence of things: in matter, in the soul, and in the eternal Art, as it is written: "Let there be, He made, and it was done." And this also corresponds to the threefold substance in Christ, Who is our ladder: His corporeal nature, His spiritual nature, and His divinity.

4. According, then, to this threefold progression, our mind has three principal faculties of perception: one is called sense or animal perception, which looks upon external corporeal things; another is spirit or reason, which looks within upon itself and what is in itself; the third is mind or intellect, which looks above itself upon that which is eternal. By these three faculties a person is disposed to ascend to God, so that he loves Him with his whole mind, with his whole heart, and with his whole soul, in which consists the perfection of the law and Christian wisdom.

5. But since each of the aforesaid modes is doubled, according as we consider God as Alpha and Omega, or according as we see God in each of these modes as through a mirror and in a mirror, or because one of these considerations can be joined to another which is contiguous to it, all these three principal stages must be raised to the number six. Hence, just as God accomplished the whole world in six days and rested on the seventh, so the smaller world of man is led in an orderly way through six progressive stages of illumination to the quiet of mystical contemplation.

6. In relation to this threefold ascent, the first stage of contemplation consists in beholding God through His vestiges in the universe; the second in beholding God in His vestiges in the sensible world. The third stage consists in beholding God through His image stamped upon our natural faculties; the fourth in beholding God in His image reformed by the gifts of grace. The fifth stage consists in beholding the divine Unity through Its primary name, which is Being; the sixth in beholding the Most Blessed Trinity in Its name, which is Good. The seventh and final stage is the mental and mystical elevation, in which rest is given to the intellect and our affection passes wholly into God.

7. He, therefore, who wishes to ascend to God must first, avoiding sin which deforms our nature, exercise his natural powers in the pursuit of virtue, in the prayer of devotion, and in the illumination of knowledge. For as no one comes to wisdom except through grace, virtue, and illumination, so no one comes to contemplation except through insight, meditation, and holy contemplation.

8. To begin with the first step: considering created things in their weight, number, and measure, we perceive that they are vestiges of the Creator. For weight gives them stability and order; number gives them distinctness and variety; measure gives them limitation and quantity. In these three modes of existence, the power, wisdom, and goodness of the Creator shine forth: power in the magnitude and vastness of things, wisdom in their beauty and variety, and goodness in their utility and bounty.

9. The vastness of things—in the immense diffusion of heavenly bodies, the extension of the earth, and the depths of the oceans—manifests the omnipotence of the Creator. The variety of things—in the diverse genera, species, and individuals of celestial, terrestrial, and aquatic creatures—manifests the manifold wisdom of the Maker. The utility of things—in the abundance of fruits, the fertility of lands, and the adaptation of creatures to the needs of man—manifests the infinite benevolence and goodness of the Father of all.

10. If we consider the sevenfold properties of creatures—namely, their origin, magnitude, multitude, beauty, plenitude, activity, and order—we shall see the invisible things of God clearly revealed from the creation of the world. For the origin of things from nothing by the command of the Word reveals divine power; their magnitude reveals immense virtue; their multitude reveals divine richness; their beauty reveals supreme harmony; their plenitude reveals abundant sufficiency; their activity reveals operating virtue; and their order reveals governing wisdom.

11. Behold, therefore, how the supreme power, wisdom, and goodness of the Creator shine forth in the corporeal world, according as the message is brought to our bodily senses by the things created. The physical universe is like a book or a mirror reflecting the Trinity: the Father as the Origin and Power, the Son as the Art and Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit as the Goodness and Order.

12. For all things created in this sensible world lead the mind of the contemplative and wise man to the eternal God, since they are the shadows, resonances, pictures, vestiges, representations, and spectacles divinely presented to our crude and sensory minds, that through sensible things which we see we may be transported to intelligible things which we do not see.

13. In these creatures, as in so many traces and signs, the eternal power, divinity, and wisdom of God are made manifest. The creature is nothing else than a kind of likeness and image of the divine wisdom, sculpted and formed by God Himself.

14. Whoever, therefore, is not enlightened by such splendors of created things is blind; whoever is not awakened by such outcries is deaf; whoever does not praise God for all these works is dumb; whoever does not perceive the First Beginning from such indications is foolish.

15. Open your eyes, therefore, prick up your spiritual ears, open your lips, and apply your heart, that in all creatures you may see, hear, praise, love, worship, glorify, and honor your God, lest perhaps the whole world rise up against you. For on this account the universe will fight against the foolish, while to the wise it will provide matter for glory, so that they may say with the Prophet: "Thou hast given me, O Lord, a delight in Thy doings, and in the works of Thy hands I shall rejoice."

sections.title: Chapter 3
sections.subtitle: Chapter II: On the Contemplation of God in His Vestiges in the Sensible World

content.text: 1. But since with respect to the mirror of sensible things it happens that we not only contemplate God through them as through vestiges, but also in them as He is in them by His essence, presence, and power, this manner of consideration constitutes the second stage of contemplation, by which we are led to contemplate God in all creatures that enter our minds through the bodily senses.

2. It must be understood, therefore, that this sensible world, called the macrocosm, enters our soul, which is called the microcosm, through the doors of the five senses, according as sensible things are perceived, delighted in, and judged. For the five senses are like five gates through which the likeness of things in the outer world enters into the soul.

3. By sight we perceive luminous and colored bodies; by hearing, sounds and voices; by smell, odors and fragrances; by taste, savors; by touch, hot and cold, wet and dry, hard and soft, rough and smooth. Through these senses, the external sensible object first produces its likeness in the medium, from the medium in the organ, from the external organ in the internal sense, and from the internal sense in the apprehending intellect.

4. After apprehension follows delight. For the sense delights in the object perceived through its abstract likeness, either on account of its beauty, as in sight; or on account of its sweetness, as in hearing and smell; or on account of its salubrity, as in taste and touch. Every delight is grounded in proportion and harmony.

5. After apprehension and delight follows judgment, by which the mind not only discerns whether a thing is white or black, sweet or bitter, but also judges why it delights and is beautiful. In this act of judgment, the mind perceives an immutable, eternal, and absolute law of proportion and harmony, which is not bounded by space or time, but is stamped upon the intellect by Eternal Truth itself.

6. If, therefore, all things that are perceived are apprehended through their generated likeness, consider that in this generation of the likeness in the medium and the sense there is manifested the eternal generation of the Word, the Image and Likeness of the invisible God, Who is eternally generated from the Father and in the fullness of time assumed our nature to lead us back to the Father.

7. And if all delight is caused by harmony and proportion, and proportion is found in numerical relations, all delight leads the mind to the supreme Proportion and Harmony, which is God Himself, the Source of all beauty, sweetness, and order.

8. Furthermore, since judgment is performed by a reason that abstracts from place, time, and mutability, and is therefore immutable, infinite, and without end, it is evident that our judgment is formed by the illumination of the unchangeable Light and the eternal Art of the Divine Mind.

9. For our intellect can judge with certainty of nothing except by the aid of that Truth which is the supreme Rule and Measure of all truth. Thus, in every act of sensory perception, delight, and judgment, the invisible attributes of the Creator are reflected and manifested.

10. Look, therefore, at the numbers and proportions in sensible things, and you will find that they are of five kinds: poetic numbers in sounds, sensible numbers in the senses, mnemonic numbers in the memory, judicial numbers in the judgment, and artificial numbers in the works of art. All these lead the mind step by step to the eternal numbers and divine proportions in the Mind of God.

11. Since all things are beautiful and in some way delightful, and beauty and delight do not exist without proportion, and proportion is primarily in numbers, all things must necessarily be full of number. For this reason number is the principal exemplar in the mind of the Creator and in things the principal vestige leading to Wisdom.

12. Since this Wisdom is the most manifest and intimate light in all things, it is astonishing that the human mind, which is surrounded by such brilliant illumination, remains so often blind to its presence, except that the soul, weighed down by the body and distracted by temporal cares, is turned away from its own true interior light.

13. Blessed are they whose hearts are purified, that they may see God shining through all created forms, praising Him in every creature, and ascending through the visible beauty of this world to the contemplation of that uncreated Beauty which never fades.

sections.title: Chapter 4
sections.subtitle: Chapter III: On the Contemplation of God through His Image Stamped on Our Natural Faculties

content.text: 1. The two aforesaid stages, by leading us into God through His vestiges whereby He shines forth in all creatures, have brought us to the threshold of our own interior house. Entering into ourselves, that is, into our mind, where the divine image shines forth, we enter the third stage of contemplation, considering the natural faculties of the soul: Memory, Intellect, and Will.

2. For the soul, entering into itself as into a spiritual sanctuary, perceives in these three faculties a trinity of operations reflecting the Most Holy Trinity: the memory retains the past, presents the present, and anticipates the future; the intellect conceives and understands truths; the will chooses and loves the good.

3. Consider the operation of memory: it retains past events by remembrance, present things by apprehension, and future things by foresight. It retains principles of sciences, immutable definitions, and eternal truths, which could not be preserved unless the memory possessed an unchangeable and everlasting light shining within it, which is the presence of God Himself.

4. Consider next the operation of intellect: it apprehends the meaning of terms, propositions, and conclusions. But the intellect cannot know the meaning of any limited or imperfect being unless it has an implicit concept of the perfect, absolute, and unlimited Being. Nor can it judge with certainty of any truth except by the light of that unchanging Truth which shines above our mind.

5. Consider thirdly the operation of the elective faculty or will: it chooses and loves that which it perceives to be good. But the will cannot desire any particular good unless it is drawn by the desire for the Supreme Good, which is the ultimate end of all our desires and the source of all beatitude.

6. See, therefore, how close the soul is to God, and how memory leads to Eternity, intellect to Truth, and the elective faculty to the Highest Good. In these three faculties the soul is an image of the Trinity: memory corresponds to the Father, the source and origin; intellect corresponds to the Son, the Word and Image; and will corresponds to the Holy Spirit, the Love and Gift of both.

7. Thus the soul, made in the image and likeness of God, is naturally ordained to know, love, and enjoy its Creator. When the mind contemplates itself in these natural faculties, it sees as in a mirror the reflection of that divine Trinity from Whom it came and to Whom it is destined to return.

sections.title: Chapter 5
sections.subtitle: Chapter IV: On the Contemplation of God in His Image Reformed by the Gifts of Grace

content.text: 1. But since not only by passing through ourselves, but also in ourselves, we can contemplate the First Principle, and this is greater than what has preceded, this consideration constitutes the fourth stage of contemplation, which considers the soul reformed and embellished by the supernatural gifts of grace.

2. For the image of God in our soul, although naturally imprinted upon its faculties, was deformed and obscured by original and actual sin. The soul, having fallen from the light of contemplation into the darkness of ignorance, concupiscence, and weakness, could not rise again by its own natural strength unless Eternal Truth, assuming human flesh in Christ, cleansed, renewed, and reformed it.

3. This reformation is accomplished through the theological virtues: Faith, Hope, and Charity. By faith the soul believes in Christ the Truth; by hope it longs for Christ the Life; by charity it is united to Christ the Way. Through these three theological virtues the soul's spiritual senses are restored.

4. When the soul is thus clothed with faith, hope, and love, it recovers its spiritual hearing and sight: it hears the words of Christ and sees the splendors of His light. It recovers its spiritual smell, smelling the fragrance of His ointment; its spiritual taste, tasting how sweet the Lord is; and its spiritual touch, embracing the Word of life.

5. Being thus reformed and adorned, the soul becomes hierarchical, ordered after the likeness of the heavenly Jerusalem and the nine angelic choirs. It is purified by devotion, illuminated by contemplation, and perfected by love, ascending through the stages of spiritual purification, illumination, and union.

6. In this state of grace, Holy Scripture is opened to the mind with wonderful clarity. The spiritual senses discern the fourfold sense of the Sacred Page: the literal, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. By the literal we know what was done; by the allegorical what we must believe; by the tropological what we must do; and by the anagogical what we must desire in eternal beatitude.

7. Our soul is thus made the temple of the Holy Spirit and the dwelling place of the Blessed Trinity, so that the Father and the Son come to it and make Their abode with it, filling it with peace, joy, and the unction of grace.

8. When the mind has attained to this state of spiritual beauty and interior order, it is prepared to pass beyond all created likenesses, whether in the external world or within itself, and to lift up its eyes to the contemplation of that divine light which is above all created intellects.

sections.title: Chapter 6
sections.subtitle: Chapter V: On the Contemplation of the Divine Unity through Its Primary Name Which Is Being

content.text: 1. It is possible to contemplate God not only outside us in His vestiges and within us in His image, but also above us in the divine light itself. This contemplation is twofold: the first regards the essential attributes of the Godhead under the name of Being (Esse / I AM WHO AM); the second regards the personal properties of the Trinity under the name of Good (Bonum).

2. When Moses asked the name of God, the Lord answered him: "I AM WHO AM. Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS hath sent me to you." This name, Being, is the primary name of God in respect to the unity of His divine essence.

3. For Being itself is so primary, simple, absolute, and necessary that it cannot even be conceived not to be. Non-being is only understood through the privation of being, just as darkness is only understood through the absence of light. Therefore Being is that which first falls into the intellect.

4. But our intellect, accustomed to the darkness of material phantasms and mutable things, often seems to see nothing when it looks upon pure Being, just as the eye of the bat is blinded by the radiance of the sun. Yet if the mind cleanses its vision, it will perceive that pure Being is eternal, most simple, most actual, most perfect, and uniquely one.

5. Behold Being itself: it is without beginning and without end, for it cannot come from non-being; it is completely indivisible and simple, having no parts or composition; it is pure act without any passive potentiality; it is supreme perfection, lacking nothing; and it is absolutely one, containing all perfection in the simplicity of its essence.

6. In this pure Being, all opposites are harmoniously reconciled without confusion: it is at once the first and the last, the most high and yet the most intimate, within all things and yet not enclosed, outside all things and yet not excluded, above all things and yet not elevated, below all things and yet not depressed.

7. It is the center and circumference of all reality, containing all things in its immense simplicity, governing all things without labor, moving all things while remaining unmoved, and renewing all things while remaining unchangeable.

8. When the mind contemplates this divine Unity, it is filled with wonder and adoration, recognizing that the First Principle is the supreme, absolute, and eternal Being from Whom, through Whom, and in Whom are all things, to Whom be glory forever.

sections.title: Chapter 7
sections.subtitle: Chapter VI: On the Contemplation of the Most Blessed Trinity in Its Name Which Is Good

content.text: 1. After having contemplated the essential attributes of the Divine Unity under the primary name of Being, our contemplation ascends to the personal properties of the Most Blessed Trinity under the name of the Good (Bonum), as Christ our Lord said: "None is good but God alone."

2. For good is essentially self-diffusive and communicative of itself. But that which is supremely good must be supremely diffusive of itself. Now supreme diffusion cannot exist unless it is actual, intrinsic, personal, consubstantial, and equal in dignity.

3. Therefore, in the Supreme Good there must be an eternal, mutual, and perfect communication: the Father eternally generates the Son, the Word and Image of His substance, communicating His whole essence; and from the Father and the Son together eternally proceeds the Holy Spirit, the Bond of mutual Love and Gift of both.

4. Behold, therefore, the highest mystery of the Christian faith: the Trinity of Persons in the Unity of Essence. In God there is the highest communicability without division of nature, the highest consubstantiality without confusion of Persons, the highest equality without subordination, the highest co-eternity without posteriority, and the highest mutual indwelling (perichoresis / circumincession) without loss of distinction.

5. Contemplate now the mystery of the Incarnation of the Word, wherein this divine Goodness and Wisdom is supremely displayed to mankind. For in Christ the highest is united to the lowest, the Creator to the creature, eternity to time, the immortal to the mortal, the infinite to the finite, and the Divine Nature to human nature in the unity of a single divine Person.

6. In Christ, the Son of God, who is the Image of the invisible God, our mind finds the culmination of its contemplation. He is the Mercy Seat placed upon the Ark of the Covenant, between the two Cherubim looking toward each other, who symbolize the two testaments and the two modes of contemplation: the contemplation of the Divine Unity (Being) and the contemplation of the Divine Trinity (Goodness).

7. When our mind looks upon Christ crucified, who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life, it has reached the summit of its ascent through the six stages of illumination. As on the sixth day man was created in the image of God, and on the sixth day the Lord Jesus suffered on the cross for man's redemption, so on this sixth step of contemplation the mind reaches its highest perfection in the vision of Christ the Crucified.

8. He who looks upon Christ with faith, hope, and burning love is ready to pass over from this world to the Father, leaving behind all intellectual and rational operations, to enter into the mystical rest of the Sabbath.

sections.title: Chapter 8
sections.subtitle: Chapter VII: On the Mental and Mystical Elevation in Which Rest Is Given to the Intellect and Affection Passes Wholly into God

content.text: 1. Now that our mind has completed the six stages of contemplation—contemplating God outside itself through His vestiges and in His vestiges, within itself through His image and in His image, above itself through the similitude of Being and through the light of Goodness—it remains that on the seventh step, as on the seventh day of creation, it should enter into the mystical Sabbath of rest.

2. In this passing over (transitus), if it is to be perfect, all intellectual activities must be left behind, and the apex of affection (apex affectus) must be wholly transferred and transformed into God. This is the mystical and secret wisdom revealed to the little ones, which no one knows except him who receives it, no one receives except him who desires it, and no one desires except him whose heart is inflamed by the Holy Spirit, Whom Christ sent upon the earth.

3. If you ask how these things come about, ask grace, not doctrine; desire, not intellect; the groaning of prayer, not the diligence of reading; the Spouse, not the teacher; God, not man; darkness, not clarity; not light, but the fire which totally inflames and transports the soul into God through excessive unction and burning affection.

4. This fire is God Himself, Whose furnace is in Jerusalem, and Christ kindled it in the fervor of His most burning Passion, which he alone truly perceives who says: "My soul hath chosen strangling, and my bones death." He who loves this death can see God, for it is true beyond all doubt: "Man shall not see Me and live."

5. Let us, therefore, die and enter into the darkness; let us impose silence upon our cares, our concupiscences, and our phantasms; let us pass over with Christ crucified from this world to the Father, that when the Father is manifested to us, we may say with Philip: "It is enough for us"; that we may hear with Paul: "My grace is sufficient for thee"; and that we may exult with David, saying: "My flesh and my heart faileth, but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion forever. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from eternity to eternity. And let all the people say: Amen, Amen."
6. Amen. Here ends the speculation of the poor man in the wilderness, composed by the Seraphic Doctor, Saint Bonaventure, on Mount La Verna, in the year of our Lord 1259.
